title: Responding to US sanctions on the International Criminal Court
gist: On 9 October 2026 the US designated the International Criminal Court itself under Executive Order 14203, freezing its assets and barring US persons from transacting with it, with a 180-day wind-down licence to April 2027. Chatham House argues ICC State Parties (led by the UK and EU) should pursue diplomacy, build a contingency plan for IT, banking and payments, and consider the 'nuclear option' of a Blocking Statute despite its legal and commercial limitations.

insights.claim: On 9 October 2026 the US escalated its ICC sanctions from individual officials to the International Criminal Court as an entity, designating it under Executive Order 14203.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Sanctioning an entire international court is a qualitative escalation that drags every counterparty of the institution into scope.
insights.quote: On 9 October 2026, the US designated the International Criminal Court under Executive Order 14203, extending its existing sanctions package on individual ICC officials to the entity itself as a whole.

insights.claim: The US designation of the ICC freezes any property owned by the Court and prohibits all transactions by US individuals or entities involving it.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: US banks, cloud and service providers must cut the Court off, threatening its operational backbone.
insights.quote: The US imposed asset freezes on any property owned by the Court and prohibited all transactions by US individuals or entities involving the ICC.

insights.claim: The US carved out limited exceptions to its ICC sanctions covering ongoing detention of some awaiting trial, pension payments, use of IT software and social media, and a 180-day wind-down period running until April 2027.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: April 2027 is the key deadline by which diplomacy must succeed or alternative service arrangements must be in place.
insights.quote: a 180-day ‘wind down’, allowing certain otherwise prohibited transactions until April 2027
insights.locator: The US has allowed certain limited exceptions

insights.claim: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio framed the sanctions as part of an ongoing campaign to 'dismantle the ICC brick by brick' and explicitly called on allies who rely on US military protection to rein in the court.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Washington is linking security guarantees to allies' stance on the ICC, raising the cost of European support for the Court.
insights.quote: We expect our allies, many of whom are part of the ICC and that rely on American service members for their defense, to rein in the court.
insights.locator: We expect our allies, many of whom

insights.claim: The ICC described the US sanctions as an attempt to obstruct justice and an assault on the rule of law and the foundations of the international legal order.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: The Court frames the dispute as existential for the rules-based order, signalling it will not accommodate US demands.
insights.quote: It is an assault on the rule of law and on the very foundations of the international legal order

themes.theme: Extraterritorial reach of the asset freeze

insights.claim: US asset-freeze obligations on the ICC bind all US persons and green card holders anywhere in the world, all US companies, any person in the US, and any transactions or data routed through the United States.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Dollar clearing and US-routed data flows give the sanctions reach well beyond US territory, including into European service providers.
insights.quote: They also apply to any transactions or data routed through the United States.

insights.claim: In practice a US designation can limit at best, and prevent at worst, nearly all financial transactions of the designated party, so unchecked sanctions could severely hamper the ICC's day-to-day operations.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: The Court's ability to pay staff, vendors and run investigations is at risk without non-US financial channels.
insights.quote: In reality, this can often limit (at best) and prevent (at worst) nearly all financial transactions of a designated person.
insights.locator: In reality, this can often limit

insights.claim: The 180-day General Licence offers at most a stay of execution plus a window for diplomacy to reverse or mitigate the sanctions, not durable relief.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: State Parties should treat the wind-down as a countdown, not a reprieve.
insights.quote: The General Licence operates to provide a wind down period, but at most provides a stay of execution and the potential for diplomatic efforts to reverse or mitigate the impact.
insights.locator: The General Licence operates to provide

insights.claim: Companies exposed to US sanctions may de-risk and stop serving the ICC well before the General Licence expires, which the US likely intends in order to disrupt the Court's investigations and operations.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Over-compliance by banks and tech vendors could cripple the Court faster than the formal legal timeline suggests.
insights.quote: companies caught by US sanctions may simply decide to stop working with the Court at any time.
insights.locator: As such, whilst the US General Licence

themes.theme: State Party response: diplomacy and contingency support

insights.claim: UK and other foreign ministers have issued a Joint Statement of unwavering support for the ICC, and the EU says it stands ready to take all necessary measures to keep the Court operating.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Rhetorical backing is in place, but concrete countermeasures have not yet been committed.
insights.quote: to take all necessary measures to ensure the Court continues to operate effectively and fulfils its indispensable mandate
insights.locator: So far, foreign ministers of the UK

insights.claim: Chatham House frames the State Parties' choice as three tracks: diplomacy, practical support for the Court, or the 'nuclear option' of a Blocking Statute.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Provides an escalation ladder for tracking how the UK and EU respond in coming months.
insights.quote: now have to decide how to respond, through diplomacy; support or the ‘nuclear option’.
insights.locator: Those countries that have signed up

insights.claim: The ICC Assembly of States Parties in December 2026 is the key forum for State Parties to review and align their response to the US.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: December is the catalyst date for a coordinated European/State Party stance.
insights.quote: The ICC’s Assembly of States Parties in December will provide an opportunity to review and align the response of the State Parties to the US.
insights.locator: The ICC’s Assembly of States Parties

insights.claim: State Parties need a comprehensive contingency plan to keep the ICC functioning, covering IT provision, banking and payment routes, in case diplomacy fails or vendors withdraw early.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Implies demand for non-US banking, payments and IT alternatives for the Court, a test case for European sovereign infrastructure.
insights.quote: That means the State Parties need a comprehensive plan to support the Court, covering everything from provision of IT to support on banking and payment routes, and everything in between.
insights.locator: Practical Support: Preparing for the Worst

insights.claim: The UK and EU Member States could invoke a Blocking Statute that would prohibit natural or legal persons from complying with the US sanctions on the ICC, a step Dutch Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen dubbed the 'nuclear option'.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: A Blocking Statute would turn a US-ICC dispute into a direct transatlantic legal conflict over sanctions compliance.
insights.quote: It would essentially prohibit any natural or legal person from complying with US sanctions.

insights.claim: Blocking Statutes have been used very rarely, mainly against US extraterritorial sanctions on countries such as Cuba and Iran.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Use for the ICC would be a novel application, with little precedent on enforcement.
insights.quote: But Blocking Statutes have only been deployed vary rarely in the past, primarily targeting US extra-territorial over-reach
insights.locator: But Blocking Statutes have only been

insights.claim: A Blocking Statute is not available to all ICC State Parties without new primary legislation, and even where it exists it is unclear the US ICC measures fit legislation designed to protect 'trading interests', leaving it open to legal challenge.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: The nuclear option is legally fragile and patchy across jurisdictions, weakening its deterrent value.
insights.quote: it is not clear that the US measures would fall squarely within the legislation which is designed to protect ‘trading interests’ against extra-territorial measures.

insights.claim: A Blocking Statute only binds those within the enacting jurisdiction, such as UK/EU nationals, UK/EU companies or those operating in the UK or EU, so it cannot stop non-European providers from cutting off the ICC.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: US-based vendors would still exit, so a Blocking Statute must be paired with European replacement services.
insights.quote: Third, it only applies to those caught by the relevant jurisdiction.

insights.claim: A Blocking Statute would put European companies in a bind, forced to breach either US sanctions or UK/EU blocking law.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Banks and multinationals with US exposure would face conflicting legal liabilities, a material compliance risk if invoked.
insights.quote: Finally, it essentially puts domestic companies between a rock and a hard place – fail to comply with US sanctions or fail to comply with the UK/EU ‘Blocking Statute’.

insights.claim: Chatham House argues that because the US has escalated from targeting ICC judges and staff to sanctioning the Court itself, supporters should now put all options, including the Blocking Statute, on the table.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Signals rising UK/EU policy-community appetite for sanctions countermeasures against Washington, an escalation risk in transatlantic relations.
insights.quote: State Parties with this potential option have not deployed it despite the US targeting of judges and Court staff
insights.locator: State Parties with this potential option
